title: Apple
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in Apple coding interviews, from Easy to Hard. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates often report from Apple interviews: strings and arrays, hashing, linked lists, trees, matrices and grids, stacks and parsing, intervals, heaps, and small design problems such as caches and counters.
- Problems are grouped Easy, Medium, and Hard so you can warm up before working on harder parsing, design, and streaming problems.
- The selection is approximate. Interview loops differ by team, and interviewers choose their own questions, so treat the list as pattern practice rather than a prediction of what you will be asked.

What to expect
- Candidates commonly describe practical problems close to the team's domain, such as parsing text, transforming images or grids, or building a small data structure with a clear API.
- You are usually expected to clarify inputs and edge cases, explain your approach and its time and space complexity, and then write clean, readable code.
- Follow-ups often probe robustness and resource use: very large inputs, deep recursion, memory limits, or making a design safe to use from several threads.
- Discussion of tradeoffs and code quality is commonly reported to matter as much as reaching a working answer.

How to prepare
- Write down your clarifying questions and a brute-force approach before you open any hint.
- Prefer iterative solutions with explicit stacks or queues when input size is unbounded, and be ready to explain why.
- For design problems, state the operations and their target complexity first, then pick the data structures that achieve them.
- After passing, explain how your solution would change if the input streamed in, did not fit in memory, or was shared between threads.
